lesson.title: Typing the Untypeable: Escape Characters
lesson.summary: A backslash followed by a letter, such as \n or \t, lets a string literal represent characters like newlines and tabs that cannot otherwise be typed directly.
lesson.body:
Some characters cannot be typed directly into a string literal, either because they have no printable symbol, like a newline or a tab, or because typing them directly would confuse Python's parser, like a quotation mark identical to the one enclosing the string. Escape characters solve this problem: a backslash followed by a specific letter or symbol stands in for a character that would otherwise be impossible or ambiguous to write, extending what you learned in String Basics about how string literals are constructed.

The most common escape character is \n, which represents a newline. When Python encounters \n inside a string, it does not print a literal backslash followed by the letter n, it inserts a single line-break character instead. Trace through print("Line one\nLine two"): Python reads the string as three logical pieces, "Line one", a newline character, and "Line two", and printing it produces two separate lines of output, "Line one" on the first and "Line two" on the second, even though the source code was a single line. Similarly, \t inserts a tab character, useful for lining up columns of text, and print("Name:\tAna") produces "Name:" followed by a tab-width gap before "Ana".

The backslash itself also solves the quotation problem. If you write "She said "hello"", Python sees the second quotation mark as the end of the string, then gets confused by the word hello sitting outside any quotes, and raises a SyntaxError. Escaping the inner quotes fixes this: "She said \"hello\"" tells Python that each \" is a literal double-quote character to include in the string, not the string's closing delimiter. Tracing it, Python builds the string character by character, treating each escaped quote as a literal " rather than a boundary, giving the final string She said "hello" when printed.

An easier fix for the quotation problem, when it applies, is simply choosing the other quote style: since Python treats 'single quotes' and "double quotes" as equivalent ways to start a string, you can write 'She said "hello"' with no escaping needed at all, because the double quotes inside are not the same character as the single quotes marking the string's boundaries. This is often clearer than escaping, though escaping is unavoidable once both quote types need to appear, or when you specifically need \n or \t.

Because the backslash is special, writing a literal backslash character requires escaping the backslash itself: \\. This becomes a genuine headache with file paths on Windows, where "C:\new\folder" is not what it looks like, because \n inside it is read as a newline escape, not the letters backslash-n. A handful of other escape sequences round out the set worth knowing: \' for a literal single quote and \\' together handle the same collision as \" does for double quotes, and \0 represents a null character, though you will rarely need it directly in ordinary text processing.

This exact backslash problem is what motivates the next chapter, Raw Strings, which offers a way to turn escaping off entirely for cases like this, so that a string containing many literal backslashes, such as a file path, does not need to be riddled with doubled-up \\ pairs just to be written correctly.
